review: An outstanding game with amazing mechanics, inspired by terraria, the student has surpassed the teacher. The devs can't progress further due to financial issues, because of Steam's stupid launch day bugs. I wish I had the cash to fund them to see where it is going. Still, it's super fun and better than most of the sandboxes.

It's been a long time since I was so amazed at an early access game. It's rough around the edges, it's easier to run on Linux via Proton than natively, the overall UX needs improvement… and yet here I am. It's obvious a great deal of passion was involved, and I hope it can continue realising its insane potential.

The special features, like creating your own spells and using monster capture gems, aren't possible to really play with without endless hours of mining for resources, the same grinding that you've seen in every other 2D mining and crafting game. By the time you've found enough resources to meaningfully try anything interesting, you'll already have explored everything worth seeing. And you'll wish everything required half as many resources as it does. 

Also, as others have pointed out, there's a partial absence of Quality of Life features and partial absence of information and a definite presence of glitches. (You can't split a stack of items in half, so feeding my chickens requires a hundred clicks to distribute their food! Mana regeneration is unbelievably slow, despite magic being a big focus, so that's more disincentive to experiment! What on Earth is going on with weapon upgrades and item scarcities!) Those all add friction, but are forgivable on their own. It's a wiki game, but there's not enough of a community for an adequate wiki to exist. 

It might be more fun for you if you have a huge appetite for this kind of game. It has bad ideas, but only a few. It has good ideas, but only a few. Maybe I missed something, or failed to find the intended entry point to engage with the systems just right, but 15 hours of Waiting For The Good Part To Begin is my limit.

Can't help but compare this to terraria although this does a lot of things that separates it far from terraria. 

There are vastly different variants of the same enemy which adds a lot of chaos to keep you on your toes. The difference between a divine enemy and a regular is night and day.  Killing or capturing them offers great rewards too.

The mechanic gear system is very interesting however I wish there was more we could do with it. 

Autofarms aren't entirely self automated which I appreciate since my take on autofarming is there should be some level of player input so the game doesn't feel like it can play itself.

Being able to capture enemies, train them, breed them, give them skills, and so many being so different from each other makes for a pretty cool monster collector.

Armor sets aren't just stat buffs but skills integrated into sets. For example, the miner armor gives you a throwable exploding pickaxe that nukes walls and enemies short range. The iron set gives you a giant spike ball that can be summoned and then launched with its hammer skill to smash enemies in a row.  Armor sets having such diverse identities adds a lot of useful variety. In terraria you're replacing armor sets constantly as you progress but here I feel the different armor sets are always useful for different situations. There needs to be a faster way to swap them though.

Weapon enchanting/relics is very cool. Gear is leveled as it's used and can be reforged which gives new life to a lot of gear.
The cooking system is absolutely ridiculous with a ton of foods and so many crops to farm. There are crafting chains for food and refinement for some items.
Animal taming is deadly but a lot of fun engaging with. I haven't played a game before where I got killed by a cow this many times while trying to kite it to a taming pen. It's a fast charging mount though which is both funny and legit useful. WAR.COW.

There is a character progression skill system and combos tied to it if you choose to use the combos, for example there is a rising screw attack right out of metroid in this. The sword flurry attack that sends you flying is awesome too. Ground slams, uppercuts etc.

The magic crafting is pretty ridiculous too. This easily has the deepest magic smithing system i've ever saw in a game. Want a fireball? nice. Want a fireball that travels at mach 10, hits a surface, splits into some crazy exploding flower pattern fireball that splits into a hundred directions while chain exploding as it hits more surfaces and enemies? faster? bigger? MORE fireball explosion chains? crazy stuff and that's just fireball, there are so many other magics you can craft with to make your magic YOUR magic.


I'm having a lot of fun with this.

Planet Centauri blends sandbox survival, RPG progression, and exploration into a colorful pixel-art world. Craft gear, fight monsters, build your base, and shape your character however you like. With plenty of freedom and a cozy-but-dangerous atmosphere, it’s a great pick for fans of open-ended 2D adventures. 🌍🛠️⚔️

Planet Centauri is an ambitious and densely packed sandbox experience that reflects both the creative freedom and the growing pains of a long-term indie project. Developed and published by Permadeath, it sets out to be more than just another 2D survival game by layering exploration, combat, crafting, automation, magic, farming, and engineering into a single, sprawling framework. While its pixel-art presentation and side-scrolling format inevitably draw comparisons to genre staples, Planet Centauri distinguishes itself through sheer mechanical scope, offering a world where curiosity and experimentation are just as important as combat prowess or resource gathering.

From the moment players enter its procedurally generated world, Planet Centauri establishes a sense of openness and possibility. Mining and crafting form the foundation, but progression quickly branches outward into numerous interconnected systems. You explore underground caverns, ancient ruins, and hostile biomes filled with enemies that possess unique traits and modifiers, making combat more varied than simple damage trading. Gear, spells, and consumables meaningfully alter how encounters play out, and permanent stat boosts gained through food and progression systems provide a tangible sense of growth tied directly to how you choose to play.

One of the game’s defining features is its breadth of player expression. Building is not limited to basic structures; instead, Planet Centauri offers hundreds of block shapes and materials that allow for detailed architectural designs and extensive terraforming. Players can shape the world around them in practical or artistic ways, whether constructing fortified bases, intricate towns, or elaborate contraptions embedded into the terrain. This creative flexibility is reinforced by systems that support farming, cooking, alchemy, and enchanting, all of which feed back into survival and combat in meaningful ways rather than existing as isolated mechanics.

Perhaps the most distinctive and ambitious aspect of Planet Centauri is its circuitry and logic system. Using soul-powered components, players can create logic gates, counters, sensors, and arithmetic systems that enable everything from automated farms to complex machines and puzzles. This “magitech” layer transforms the game into a playground for engineering-minded players, blurring the line between survival sandbox and creative simulation. While entirely optional, it adds enormous depth for those willing to learn it, offering possibilities rarely seen in 2D sandbox games.

The game also encourages interaction with its ecosystem through monster taming and breeding. Creatures encountered in the world can be captured, trained, and housed, each bringing different abilities and traits. Breeding mechanics allow inherited attributes, adding long-term planning and personalization to companion management. These systems lend personality to the world and create additional goals beyond simple progression, making the journey feel less linear and more player-driven.

That said, Planet Centauri’s greatest strength—its abundance of systems—is also its biggest weakness. Many mechanics feel promising but unevenly realized, with limited depth or unclear feedback that can make them feel incomplete. New players are often confronted with a steep learning curve, compounded by sparse tutorials and interfaces that struggle to clearly communicate the purpose and interaction of so many features. Quality-of-life limitations, occasional balance issues, and inconsistent polish across systems can make the experience feel overwhelming or unfocused, particularly for players expecting a more streamlined sandbox.

Combat and exploration, while generally enjoyable, can also feel inconsistent. Enemy difficulty spikes, underexplained modifiers, and occasional clunky interactions sometimes disrupt the flow of progression. Yet these issues coexist with moments of genuine discovery—finding rare items, uncovering hidden structures, or devising a clever mechanical solution—that remind players why the sandbox genre remains so compelling. Planet Centauri frequently rewards patience and experimentation, even if it doesn’t always guide players clearly toward those rewards.

The game’s long development history and eventual full release add further context to its identity. Years in early access shaped a project that grew organically, sometimes faster in ideas than refinement. As a result, Planet Centauri feels less like a tightly curated experience and more like a vast toolbox shaped by experimentation and community feedback. This makes it especially appealing to players who enjoy setting their own goals and tolerating rough edges in exchange for creative freedom.

Ultimately, Planet Centauri is a game defined by ambition rather than polish. It does not aim to compete with genre giants through refinement alone, but through variety, flexibility, and the joy of discovery. For players who value sandbox depth, experimentation, and systems-driven gameplay—and who are willing to accept imperfections as part of that journey—it offers a rich and often rewarding experience. While it may not fully realize every idea it introduces, Planet Centauri stands as a bold, eclectic sandbox that invites players to explore, build, and invent in a world that rewards imagination as much as survival.

Rating: 7/10

Planet Centauri es un sandbox de aventura y supervivencia en 2D que destaca por su enorme profundidad y posibilidades. Su mundo es vibrante, lleno de criaturas, biomas y sistemas complejos que invitan a la exploración constante. La personalización del personaje, la construcción y la magia ofrecen una libertad creativa que lo hace muy entretenido.

Sin embargo, también es un juego exigente: su curva de aprendizaje es notablemente pronunciada y muchas de sus mecánicas requieren tiempo para dominarse. Esto puede resultar abrumador al inicio, pero quienes perseveran encuentran una experiencia rica y gratificante. En resumen, es un título muy divertido, pero pensado para jugadores que disfrutan los desafíos y la experimentación.

Você sabe quando você já jogou tudo o que Terraria tinha para jogar e você começa experimentar mods curiosos para se divertir? Planet Centauri parece exatamente isso. O jogo é uma cópia escancarada de Terraria que tenta incluir muitas coisas novas, mas não executa nem balanceia elas bem a ponto de serem divertidas e coerentes.

É uma pena, porque o jogo tem um potencial incrível, mas ele tenta abraçar muitas mecânicas ao mesmo tempo e acaba parecendo raso e repetitivo. O endgame é um grind insuportável que me desanimou, apesar de ver outros jogadores na internet que tiveram dedicação de fazer coisas incríveis -- eu não tive.

Deixo aqui minha resenha agridoce, porque não acho que o jogo mereça um review negativo. Mas também não acho que o Planet Centauri seja um jogo para todo mundo, apenas para aqueles muito apaixonados por Terraria e que procuram experiências diferentes.
